# Logical Operator Algebra {#sec-logical-algebra}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

A logical plan is what the engine has decided your query *means*,
expressed as a directed acyclic graph of operators. Each operator
declares its inputs and its output. The graph is the engine's
internal language for "what to compute"; everything from
optimisation through code generation operates on it.

This chapter walks through the operator vocabulary, the structural
properties of the graph (immutable, type-erased, schema-annotated),
and the conventions that recur in later parts of the book.

---

## 6.1 The operator family {#sec-operator-family}

Every logical operator in NebulaStream lives in
`nes-logical-operators/include/Operators/`. The full list as of the
pinned commit:

| Operator | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `SourceDescriptorLogicalOperator` | Bound source; produces tuples |
| `InlineSinkLogicalOperator` | Bound sink; consumes tuples |
| `ProjectionLogicalOperator` | Selects/computes a subset of fields |
| `SelectionLogicalOperator` | Filters tuples by a predicate |
| `UnionLogicalOperator` | Concatenates two streams of compatible schema |
| `JoinLogicalOperator` | Stream-stream join, typically windowed |
| `WindowedAggregationLogicalOperator` | Aggregate per window |

Eight operators. Notably absent:

- **No DISTINCT.** Use windowed aggregation with a no-op aggregate.
- **No subqueries.** No correlated joins, no `EXISTS`. The streaming
  model does not lend itself to them.
- **No SORT.** Streams are unordered modulo watermark progress; a
  total order is not a primitive.

This minimalism is, again, intentional. Streaming queries are
shallow; complicating the algebra adds optimiser surface without
adding meaningful workloads.

---

## 6.2 The C++20 concept twist {#sec-concept-design}

The operator hierarchy is not a virtual class hierarchy. Instead,
NebulaStream uses C++20 concepts to define what a logical operator
*is*, then type-erases concrete operators behind a wrapper:

```cpp
// nes-logical-operators/include/Operators/LogicalOperator.hpp
template <typename T>
concept LogicalOperatorConcept = requires(T t) {
    { t.explain() } -> std::convertible_to<std::string>;
    { t.getChildren() }
        -> std::convertible_to<std::vector<LogicalOperator>>;
    { t.withChildren(std::vector<LogicalOperator>{}) }
        -> std::convertible_to<LogicalOperator>;
    { t.getOutputSchema() }
        -> std::convertible_to<Schema>;
    { t.getInputSchemas() }
        -> std::convertible_to<std::vector<Schema>>;
};
```

A type satisfies the concept if it has those five methods.
`LogicalOperator` itself is a type-erased reference type: under the
hood it stores an `any`-like container plus a vtable of pointers to
those five concept methods, so the cost of dispatch is the same as
a virtual call but the *concrete operator types* never need to
inherit from anything.

The benefit is composition. A user-defined operator only needs to
satisfy the concept; it does not need to inherit from
`LogicalOperator`. Adding a new operator (say, a hypothetical
`LimitLogicalOperator` from Chapter 5's exercise) is a class with
five methods, not a class deriving from a chain of bases.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: how Calcite does this"}
Apache Calcite uses traditional inheritance: every operator
extends `RelNode` (a 4000-line virtual class) and its rule engine
walks a class hierarchy. The result is faster to grow at scale
(easier to add framework-wide functionality) but harder to extend
from outside (every new operator inherits a lot of implicit
contract).

NebulaStream's concept-based approach is the inverse trade. Easier
to extend from outside; needs more discipline at the framework
level because the contract is enforced only at use sites, not in a
shared base class.
:::

---

## 6.3 The plan as an immutable DAG {#sec-immutable-dag}

A `LogicalPlan` is a vector of root operators. The DAG is read by
walking children:

```cpp
// nes-logical-operators/include/Plans/LogicalPlan.hpp
class LogicalPlan {
public:
    LogicalPlan() = delete;
    explicit LogicalPlan(LogicalOperator rootOperator);
    explicit LogicalPlan(QueryId queryId,
                         std::vector<LogicalOperator> rootOperators);
    [[nodiscard]] QueryId getQueryId() const;
    [[nodiscard]] std::vector<LogicalOperator> getRootOperators() const;
    [[nodiscard]] LogicalPlan withRootOperators(
        const std::vector<LogicalOperator>& operators) const;
private:
    QueryId queryId = INVALID_QUERY_ID;
    std::vector<LogicalOperator> rootOperators;
    std::string originalSql;
};
```

The plan is *immutable*. There is no `setRootOperators`; instead,
`withRootOperators` returns a new plan. Optimiser rules accept a
plan and return a transformed plan; they never mutate in place.

Two consequences fall out of this.

**Plans are cheap to share.** A plan in mid-optimisation can be
reasoned about by multiple rule engines without any defensive
copying. Each rule's output is a different plan; they coexist.

**Plans are cheap to inspect.** A debugger or logger can dump a
plan without worrying about race conditions or visiting an in-
progress mutation. We use this in Chapter 9 when we walk through
optimiser-rule output.

The cost is allocation: every transformation allocates a new top-
level `LogicalPlan` object, plus any operator nodes that changed.
Because operators inside the plan are reference-counted (they share
their type-erased payloads through `shared_ptr`-like pointers),
unchanged subtrees are shared. The actual copy cost is small.

---

## 6.4 Stateful operators carry extra metadata {#sec-stateful-metadata}

Stateless operators (Projection, Selection, Union) carry only
their input and output schemas. Stateful operators carry more.

The `WindowedAggregationLogicalOperator` is representative:

```cpp
// nes-logical-operators/include/Operators/Windows/WindowedAggregationLogicalOperator.hpp
class WindowedAggregationLogicalOperator final : public OriginIdAssigner {
public:
    WindowedAggregationLogicalOperator(
        std::vector<FieldAccessLogicalFunction> groupingKey,
        std::vector<std::shared_ptr<WindowAggregationLogicalFunction>>
            aggregationFunctions,
        std::shared_ptr<Windowing::WindowType> windowType);
    [[nodiscard]] bool isKeyed() const;
    [[nodiscard]] std::vector<std::shared_ptr<WindowAggregationLogicalFunction>>
        getWindowAggregation() const;
    [[nodiscard]] std::shared_ptr<Windowing::WindowType> getWindowType() const;
    [[nodiscard]] std::vector<FieldAccessLogicalFunction>
        getGroupingKeys() const;
};
```

Three pieces of metadata: a grouping key (possibly empty for global
aggregation), a list of aggregation functions, and a window type.
The window type is a separate `Windowing::WindowType` hierarchy
covering tumbling, sliding, and session windows. Chapter 7 uses
this object pervasively when discussing watermark-driven triggering.

`OriginIdAssigner` is a base mixin: stateful operators *create
new origins*. The output of an aggregation is logically a new
stream, with a fresh `OriginId`; downstream operators reason about
its watermarks independently of the input streams. We will see
this machinery in Chapter 7.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 6.1: a windowed aggregation plan"}
For `SELECT key, AVG(speed) FROM vehicles GROUP BY key WINDOW
TUMBLING(creationTS, SIZE 1 SECOND) INTO alerts`, the bound plan
shape is:

```
SinkLogicalOperator(alerts)
└── WindowedAggregationLogicalOperator(
        groupingKey={vehicles$key},
        aggregations=[Avg(vehicles$speed)],
        window=TumblingWindow(creationTS, 1s))
    └── SourceDescriptorLogicalOperator(vehicles)
```

Three operators. Note that `SELECT key` and `SELECT
AVG(speed)` are not separate Projection nodes — they are
absorbed into the aggregation operator's grouping key and
aggregation functions, respectively. This is a small but
worth-noting fact: NebulaStream's algebra does not separate
"compute the aggregation" from "project the result"; they are one
operator.
:::

## 6.5 The trait set: optimiser scratchpad {#sec-trait-set}

Each operator carries a *trait set* — a set of decorations that
optimiser passes attach to record decisions. Examples:

- `JoinImplementationTypeTrait` — set by `DecideJoinTypesRule`,
  records whether the join should be a hash join or a nested-loop
  join.
- `MemoryLayoutTrait` — set by `DecideMemoryLayoutRule`, records
  the chosen row/columnar layout.
- `OriginIdTrait` — set by `OriginIdInferenceRule`, records the
  origin identifier of the operator's output.

Traits are a generic mechanism. Each trait is a class; an operator
holds a `TraitSet` (essentially a typed map) and exposes
`getTrait<T>()` to retrieve a specific trait if present. Traits are
how optimiser passes communicate downstream without baking decisions
into operator constructors.

We will see traits used extensively in Chapter 9 (rule-based
optimisation) and Chapter 10 (physical lowering).

---

## 6.6 Reading a plan {#sec-reading-plan}

A `LogicalPlan` has an `explain()` method that produces a textual
representation, useful for debugging and tests. The output is
indented to show the tree structure:

```
SinkLogicalOperator(name=alerts, schema={vehicles$key: UINT64, avgSpeed: FLOAT64})
└── WindowedAggregationLogicalOperator(window=Tumbling(1s), groupingKey=[vehicles$key], aggregations=[Avg(vehicles$speed)])
    └── SourceDescriptorLogicalOperator(name=vehicles, schema={…})
```

Most systests assert on this textual representation. If you change
an operator's schema or its trait set, the explain string changes,
and a test failure tells you something visible has shifted.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch6-summary}

NebulaStream's logical algebra is small (eight operators), built on
C++20 concepts rather than virtual inheritance, immutable (a
transformation produces a new plan), and decorated by an optimiser-
extensible trait set. Stateful operators carry extra metadata —
window type, grouping key, aggregation functions — and create new
origins so downstream operators can reason about their watermarks
independently. The minimalism of the algebra is matched by the
minimalism of the optimiser (Chapter 9), and the immutability is
matched by the pure-function style of the optimiser phases.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch6-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 6.1: explain three plans"}
For each of these queries, write down (or run and capture) the
expected `explain()` output:

1. `SELECT value FROM demo INTO result;`
2. `SELECT value FROM demo WHERE value > 100 INTO result;`
3. `SELECT key, COUNT(*) FROM demo GROUP BY key WINDOW
   TUMBLING(ts, SIZE 1 SEC) INTO counts;`

How many operators in each plan? Which carry trait sets?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 6.2: confirm immutability"}
In a debugger, set a breakpoint at the entry of any optimiser
rule's `apply` method (e.g., `RedundantProjectionRemovalRule::apply`).
Inspect the input plan's address. Run the rule. Inspect the
returned plan's address. Confirm they differ.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 6.3: implement a no-op operator"}
Sketch (no need to compile) a class `NoOpLogicalOperator` that
implements the `LogicalOperatorConcept`: passes its input through
unchanged. What are the five required methods, what does each
return? You should be able to write the class in 30 lines.
:::
